A library only works because someone keeps things findable. Being responsible isn't dramatic. It's putting the right book back on the right shelf, every time.
Someone thinks their wallet was stolen. Look for evidence before pointing fingers.
'It has to be someone here! It's gone!'
Three people nearby. All calm. All willing to talk.
'I sat right here. Then I got up. Then it was gone!'
'We didn't see anyone take anything. But we were here the whole time.'
There's a gap. Something is wedged there.
Search around the bench for the wallet
Nobody stole anything — probably. Look before you accuse.
You reach into the gap and pull out the wallet — untouched, just fallen. The owner covers their mouth: 'Oh no. I nearly blamed someone.'
The wallet fell — nobody took it. If I'd trusted the owner's guess, three innocent people would have been branded thieves. Truth first. Blame later, if ever.
A student accidentally handed in someone else's homework. Find the real owner and return it.
'I grabbed the wrong notebook from the shared table. Now they'll think I copied.'
The mix-up notebook has a name half-scratched off and a doodle in the corner.
Several students nearby. Each carries their own notebook — check the doodles.
'Please. I'm not a cheat. I just picked up the wrong one.'
A small star doodle. That's someone's signature style.
One of them has stars all over their bag. That's your person.
Return the notebook to its true owner
Look at each classmate's things. Which one signs their work with tiny stars?
You hand it over. They light up: 'You found it! And thanks for saying it wasn't stolen — that means a lot.'
Flowers, not stars. Not their notebook.
Perfect match — same tiny stars as on the cover.
One student almost got labeled a cheat because of a mix-up. Honesty means owning your mistake AND helping fix the story — not just leaving the truth to sort itself out.
Everyone blames one kid for the broken window. Check the evidence yourself before you agree.
'I wasn't even here! But nobody believes me.'
None near the window. The accused kid never approached it.
A ball rests on the ground twenty meters away — not thrown, just sitting.
A flag whips hard. There was a strong gust an hour ago.
'They said it was me because I play in this alley. I wasn't here today.'
The ground under the window is undisturbed. No footprints. Nobody stood here recently.
It's still. No spin. No signs it was thrown at the window — it's too far.
A loose shutter above the window bangs in the wind. That shutter — that could break glass.
Pick every piece of evidence that clears the accused
You need three facts pointing away from the kid — not just one.
You lay the three facts out. The crowd goes quiet. Someone finally says: 'We owe you an apology.' The kid exhales for what feels like the first time.
Solid — if they broke it, they'd have stood there.
Right — no way that ball hit the window.
Yes — the shutter banging broke the glass.
They often play in this alley
Being nearby isn't proof of guilt.
Everyone was certain. Everyone was wrong. The wind broke the window, not the kid. Facts don't care how loud the crowd is. Always check before you agree.
Kids are arguing over the swings. Set up a fair rotation so everyone gets a turn.
Five kids. Two swings. That's the whole problem.
Each kid tells you when they got here. First-come-first-served is the fairest baseline.
They actually want a fair system. They just don't know how to make one.
Two swings. Rotation every 3 minutes will get everyone a turn quickly.
Aya first, then Ben, then Cai, then Dee, then Eli. They're honest about it.
Nobody is trying to cut in. They just need a plan.
Line the kids up in fair order
Fairest rule here: whoever arrived first, goes first. Arrange them.
You call the order out. Nobody argues. Aya goes first. Everyone will get a turn in eight minutes flat.
Fairness isn't complicated when you actually ask people. First-come-first-served, three minutes each, everyone smiling by minute eight. Rules can be gentle.
There aren't enough snacks. Give each child their fair share — no favorites, no seconds.
You count twelve muffins in the basket.
Four hungry faces. That's three each — clean division.
One kid tries to charm you. Fairness is fairness — same share for everyone.
Twelve. Even number. That divides cleanly.
Everyone gets the same. That's the whole point.
Give each child exactly three snacks
Twelve snacks. Four kids. Three each — no more, no less.
Every kid holds three muffins. Everyone smiles. Nobody counts a neighbor's plate — because they don't need to.
Every kid gets three. Not one more, not one less.
Sharing equally sounds simple. In practice, it means resisting the temptation to give more to the kid who charms you. Fairness = same rules, same share, for everyone.
Five robots need charging. Only one bay is free at a time. Fair means helping the neediest first.
They're waiting to see what you decide. This is on you.
One is about to shut down
The 5% unit is trembling. Every second matters.
No fights — they trust you'll be fair.
It won't last another two minutes without a charge.
Order the robots by charging priority
Fairness sometimes means: whoever needs it most, goes first.
The 5% unit plugs in and steadies. The 70% unit nods approvingly: 'I can wait. That's what fair looks like.'
Equal isn't always fair. The unit at 5% needed the plug more than the one at 70%. Fair means noticing who's suffering — and going to them first.
A child is scared to cross a broken bridge. Place planks over the gaps and walk with them.
'The gaps are too big. I can't jump.'
Count them: four missing sections between here and the other side.
Exactly four sturdy planks piled beside the bridge. Someone left them for this.
'I can't. I've tried. Please don't make me.'
Four gaps. Four planks. That's not a coincidence.
One plank per gap. When it's whole, you'll cross together.
You hold their hand. They take the first step. Then the second. Then they're running across, laughing.
